# Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention

Karthik Viswanathan ^(†)^(†)thanks: Correspondence to
[vkarthik095@gmail.com](mailto:vkarthik095@gmail.com).
Affiliation: Verified Mechanisms Affiliation: MATS Research    Plamen
Dimitrov Affiliation: Verified Mechanisms    Stefano Rocca
Affiliation: Verified Mechanisms    Sarayu Sirikonda
Affiliation: Verified Mechanisms Affiliation: University of California,
Berkeley

###### Abstract

Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer
architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads
remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only
transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head
complexity $`H^{\ast}(f)`$ of a Boolean function $`f`$ as the minimum
number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact
linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general
threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for
which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we
independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the
function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even
when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent
characterization of [Hsu and Xu (2026)](#bib.bib25) in a model without
positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general
threshold-degree bound with the classical result of [Aspnes et al.
(1994)](#bib.bib9). These results were discovered and formalized by a
frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and
machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level
questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean
formalization and research traces publicly available to support
agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic
interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the
capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to
develop an understanding of transformer architectures.

Keywords: mechanistic interpretability, expressivity, formal
verification, autonomous research.

## 1 Introduction

Mechanistic interpretability is an important component of a broader
toolkit for AI safety and oversight [Bengio et al. (2026)](#bib.bib12).
Theoretical mechanistic interpretability works [Elhage et al.
(2021)](#bib.bib13); [Elhage et al. (2022)](#bib.bib14); [Geshkovski et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib15) have shaped empirical interpretability [Olsson
et al. (2022)](#bib.bib16); [Cunningham et al. (2023)](#bib.bib17);
[Viswanathan et al. (2026)](#bib.bib18) by providing useful
abstractions, and principled starting points for experimentation.
However, developing this kind of theory has been demanding, requiring
sustained expert effort to work through the underlying mathematics.
Recent advances in language models for mathematical reasoning and formal
theorem proving [Tsoukalas et al. (2026)](#bib.bib19); [Alon et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib20); [Yang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib11) create an
opportunity to accelerate the development of rigorous theory for
mechanistic interpretability.

Such theory would be especially valuable for multi-head attention
([Vaswani et al., 2017](#bib.bib1)), since a more fundamental account of
how it transforms the residual stream could support mechanistic
interpretability in both models at scale and toy models. In models at
scale, a theory of how attention heads transform and combine features
could inform theoretically grounded feature-decomposition tools
([Cunningham et al., 2023](#bib.bib17); [Shafran et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)), by relating the features the probes recover to
computations that the architecture can implement. For toy models, a
theory of multi-head attention can provide a principled basis for
interpreting and generalizing empirical findings about how learned
computations are distributed across attention heads ([Nanda et al.,
2023](#bib.bib21); [Piotrowski et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)). For instance,
the problem studied here arose from an empirical finding in a one-layer
transformer trained on modular addition [Nanda et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib21): parity was only weakly linearly decodable from
individual head outputs, but became nearly perfectly decodable when the
head outputs were combined. This suggested that parity was implemented
as a distributed computation across heads, motivating us to ask whether
single-head attention faces a structural expressivity barrier.

##### Related work

Transformer expressivity has been studied through logical
characterizations, approximation theory, and analyses of formal
languages and Boolean functions ([Weiss et al., 2021](#bib.bib2); [Yang
and Chiang, 2024](#bib.bib4); [Sälzer et al., 2026](#bib.bib28);
[Kajitsuka and Sato, 2024](#bib.bib5); [Hahn, 2020](#bib.bib3);
[Kozachinskiy et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Hsu, 2026](#bib.bib24); [Köver
et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)). [Yu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib27) establish
upper and lower bounds on the parameter complexity required for
$`\epsilon`$-approximation as the number of heads varies, while [Hsu
(2026)](#bib.bib24) establishes lower bounds on the head count for
representing $`n`$-bit parity with one-layer transformers. In concurrent
work, [Hsu and Xu (2026)](#bib.bib25) also obtain the exact head-count
characterization for symmetric functions in a model without positional
embeddings. [Rajaraman et al. (2026)](#bib.bib26) also study head
complexity, proving that $`n`$-bit parity requires exactly $`n`$ heads
and establishing upper and lower bounds for general Boolean functions.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Relation to Concurrent Work ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
compares these concurrent results with our work.

Despite this progress, deriving general expressivity guarantees for
multi-head attention remains technically demanding because tracking even
a single layer involves multiple attention head updates and their
interactions. Agent-assisted mathematical reasoning can help navigate
this analytical complexity, while formal verification provides a
rigorous check on the resulting claims. We apply this framework to a
concrete expressivity question for Boolean functions:

> For a Boolean function $`f`$, what is the minimum number of attention
> heads needed to represent $`f`$ in a single attention layer?

## 2 Autonomous Research Result

##### Setup

We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer based on multi-head
attention ([Vaswani et al., 2017](#bib.bib1)), followed by a linear
threshold readout at the position of a dedicated query token $`q`$, as
illustrated in
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Setup ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention").
For an input $`\mathbf{x}`$ comprising $`n`$ bits, let
$`\mathcal{I}:=[n]\cup\{q\}`$ denote the set of sequence positions, and
let $`\mathbf{u}_{j}(\mathbf{x})`$ denote the input representation at
position $`j`$, obtained by adding its token and positional embeddings.
The query representation $`\mathbf{u}_{q}`$ is independent of the input
because its token and position are fixed. Each head $`h`$ applies query,
key, and value projections $`W_{Q}^{(h)},W_{K}^{(h)},W_{V}^{(h)}`$,
followed by an output projection $`W_{O}^{(h)}`$ that maps its result
back to the model space.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Model Details ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives the full parameterization and dimensions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: One-layer attention-only model. The input consists of $`n`$
bit tokens followed by a dedicated query token $`q`$, which also serves
as the readout position. Each position is represented by the sum of a
token embedding and a positional embedding, and the resulting embedded
sequence is shared by all $`H`$ heads. The heads update all positions in
parallel, but the linear readout uses only position $`q`$. At this
position, the head outputs are added to the residual $`\mathbf{u}_{q}`$,
yielding $`\mathbf{h}_{q}(\mathbf{x})`$. Thus, $`f`$ is represented
exactly when the inputs labelled $`0`$ and $`1`$ are linearly separable
at the readout position $`\mathbf{h}_{q}(\mathbf{x})`$, and
$`H^{\ast}(f)`$ is the minimum $`H`$ for which this occurs.

The final output at the query position is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathbf{h}_{q}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{u}_{q}+\sum_{h=1}^{H}W_{O}^{(h)}\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\exp\!\left(\left\langle W_{K}^{(h)}\mathbf{u}_{j}(\mathbf{x}),W_{Q}^{(h)}\mathbf{u}_{q}\right\rangle\right)W_{V}^{(h)}\mathbf{u}_{j}(\mathbf{x})}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\exp\!\left(\left\langle W_{K}^{(h)}\mathbf{u}_{j}(\mathbf{x}),W_{Q}^{(h)}\mathbf{u}_{q}\right\rangle\right)}.
``` |  | (1) |

We say that $`f`$ is *exactly representable* with $`H`$ heads if there
exist model parameters of the form specified in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Model Details ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention"),
and a linear readout $`(\mathbf{w},\tau)`$ such that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\forall\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n},\qquad\bigl[f(\mathbf{x})=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left\langle\mathbf{w},\mathbf{h}_{q}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle>\tau\bigr].
``` |  | (2) |

Adding positional embeddings is a seemingly modest but consequential
extension: they can break permutation invariance and enlarge the
representable function class. This allows us to study nonsymmetric
Boolean functions beyond the setting considered by [Hsu and Xu
(2026)](#bib.bib25).

### 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity

The *head complexity* of $`f`$ is the least number of heads in an exact
representation:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
H^{\ast}(f)=\min\{H:f\text{ is exactly representable by an }H\text{-head model}\}.
``` |  | (3) |

Each head contributes one linear-fractional function after readout
([Charnes and Cooper, 1962](#bib.bib8)), giving an equivalent
characterization of $`H^{\ast}(f)`$ without tracking the embeddings and
weight matrices in
Equations ([1](#S2.E1 "In Setup ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention"))
and ([2](#S2.E2 "In Setup ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")).
We call this one-head building block an atom.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

###### Definition 2 (Linear-fractional complexity).

The *linear-fractional complexity* of $`f`$, denoted
$`L_{\mathrm{frac}}(f)`$, is the least nonnegative integer $`H`$ for
which there exist linear-fractional atoms $`\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{H}`$
and a constant $`c\in\mathbb{R}`$ such that, for every
$`\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}`$,
$`c+\sum_{h=1}^{H}\phi_{h}(\mathbf{x})>0\Longleftrightarrow f(\mathbf{x})=1`$.

###### Theorem 1 (Linear-fractional normal form).

Fix $`H\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}`$. A function
$`S:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}`$ is the scalar score
$`S(\mathbf{x})=\langle\mathbf{w},\mathbf{h}_{q}(\mathbf{x})\rangle-\tau`$
of an $`H`$-head model in our setting, with unrestricted model and head
dimensions, if and only if it has the form

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
S(\mathbf{x})=c+\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{\mathbf{A}_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b_{h}}{\mathbf{C}_{h}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+d_{h}},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n},
``` |  | (5) |

where $`c\in\mathbb{R}`$ and each tuple
$`(\mathbf{A}_{h},b_{h},\mathbf{C}_{h},d_{h})`$ is admissible in the
sense of
Definition [1](#Thmdefinition1 "Definition 1 (Linear-fractional atom). ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention").
Each head contributes one atom, and any collection of $`H`$ atoms can be
realized jointly by $`H`$ heads using shared token and positional
embeddings. Consequently, for every Boolean function $`f`$,

|     |                                   |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       H^{\ast}(f)=L_{\mathrm{frac}}(f).
       ```                                |     |

An atom thus gives a compact, exact representation of a head’s
contribution after scalar readout. The full model’s score is the sum of
these atoms and the constant $`c`$, which accounts for the fixed query
residual and readout threshold.

#### 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds

For notational simplicity, let us fix a head and suppress its head
index. Let $`\mathbf{e}_{0}`$ and $`\mathbf{e}_{1}`$ be the token
embeddings for bits zero and one, and let $`\mathbf{p}_{i}`$ be the
positional embedding at input position $`i`$. With
$`\Delta\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{e}_{1}-\mathbf{e}_{0}`$, the input vector at
position $`i`$, before attention, is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{e}_{x_{i}}+\mathbf{p}_{i}=\mathbf{e}_{0}+\mathbf{p}_{i}+x_{i}\Delta\mathbf{e}.
``` |  |

Thus $`\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x})`$ combines the token and positional
embeddings and depends on the input $`\mathbf{x}`$ only through its
$`i`$-th bit $`x_{i}`$.

Using this head’s key and query projections, $`W_{K}`$ and $`W_{Q}`$,
the logit for attending from the query token to position $`i`$ is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\left\langle W_{K}\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x}),W_{Q}\mathbf{u}_{q}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x}),W_{K}^{\top}W_{Q}\mathbf{u}_{q}\right\rangle.
``` |  |

The vector $`W_{K}^{\top}W_{Q}\mathbf{u}_{q}`$ is fixed as the input
varies: the model weights are fixed, and the query representation
$`\mathbf{u}_{q}`$ is input-independent. The logit is therefore a dot
product of $`\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x})`$ with a fixed vector, making it
linear in $`\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x})`$. Likewise, applying the value
projection $`W_{V}`$, output projection $`W_{O}`$, and scalar readout
$`\mathbf{w}`$ gives
$`s_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\langle\mathbf{w},W_{O}W_{V}\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x})\rangle`$.
This is also linear in $`\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x})`$ because all three
maps are linear. Substituting the expression for
$`\mathbf{u}_{i}(\mathbf{x})`$ gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\kappa_{i}+ax_{i},\qquad s_{i}(\mathbf{x})=m_{i}+\beta x_{i}.
``` |  |

Here $`\kappa_{i}`$ and $`m_{i}`$ are the logit and scalar value when
$`x_{i}=0`$, while $`a`$ and $`\beta`$ are their changes when the bit
switches to one. These changes are shared across positions because
switching any input bit adds the same vector $`\Delta\mathbf{e}`$ to its
embedding.

##### Weighted scalar values (numerator).

Exponentiating the logit gives the unnormalized attention weight
$`\exp(\ell_{i}(\mathbf{x}))=\rho_{i}\alpha^{x_{i}}`$, where
$`\rho_{i}=\exp(\kappa_{i})>0`$ and $`\alpha=\exp(a)>0`$. Multiplying
this weight by the corresponding scalar value
$`s_{i}(\mathbf{x})=m_{i}+\beta x_{i}`$ gives
$`\rho_{i}\alpha^{x_{i}}(m_{i}+\beta x_{i})`$. This product is affine in
$`x_{i}`$, using $`\alpha^{x_{i}}=1+(\alpha-1)x_{i}`$ and
$`x_{i}^{2}=x_{i}`$ on Boolean inputs. Let $`\ell_{q}`$ and $`s_{q}`$
denote the query token’s logit and scalar value, both of which are
constant because $`\mathbf{u}_{q}`$ is fixed. Summing the weighted
scalar values over the input positions and the query token gives the
affine numerator

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
N(\mathbf{x})=\exp(\ell_{q})s_{q}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\rho_{i}\alpha^{x_{i}}(m_{i}+\beta x_{i})=\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b.
``` |  |

##### Unnormalized attention weights (denominator).

The denominator sums the same unnormalized attention weights over the
input positions and the query token. Since
$`\alpha^{x_{i}}=1+(\alpha-1)x_{i}`$ on Boolean inputs, this sum is also
affine:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D(\mathbf{x})=\exp(\ell_{q})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\rho_{i}\alpha^{x_{i}}=\mathbf{C}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+d.
``` |  |

This denominator is strictly positive because every unnormalized
attention weight is positive.

The head’s scalar contribution is obtained by dividing the weighted
scalar-value sum by the total attention weight. Combining the two
expressions therefore gives the linear-fractional form of
Definition [1](#Thmdefinition1 "Definition 1 (Linear-fractional atom). ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention"):

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\phi(\mathbf{x})=\frac{N(\mathbf{x})}{D(\mathbf{x})}=\frac{\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b}{\mathbf{C}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+d}.
``` |  |

Conversely, every admissible tuple determines valid attention weights
and values. With unrestricted model width, separate coordinate blocks
allow all $`H`$ heads to realize their prescribed atoms within the same
shared embeddings.
Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Linear-Fractional Normal Form ‣ Appendix E Proofs of the Main Results ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives both constructions and proves the exact coefficient
characterization.

###### Corollary 1 (One head).

$`H^{\ast}(f)=0`$ if and only if $`f`$ is constant, and
$`H^{\ast}(f)\leq 1`$ if and only if $`f`$ is a linear threshold
function: there exist reals $`\theta_{0},\ldots,\theta_{n}`$ such that,
for every $`\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}`$,
$`f(\mathbf{x})=1\Longleftrightarrow\theta_{0}+\sum_{i}\theta_{i}x_{i}>0`$.

Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 One-Head Characterization ‣ Appendix E Proofs of the Main Results ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives the proof. Parity is not a linear threshold function, so
Corollary [1](#Thmcorollary1 "Corollary 1 (One head). ‣ Unnormalized attention weights (denominator). ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
already gives a structural reason why parity was not linearly decodable
from single heads in the modular-addition model of
Section [1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention").

We next relate head complexity to threshold degree. Let
$`\deg_{\pm}(f)`$ be the minimum degree of a real polynomial that
sign-represents¹¹ 1 A real polynomial $`P`$ *sign-represents* $`f`$ if,
for every $`\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}`$,
$`P(\mathbf{x})>0\Longleftrightarrow f(\mathbf{x})=1`$. $`f`$ on the
Boolean cube ([Minsky and Papert, 1969](#bib.bib7)).

###### Theorem 2 (Threshold-degree lower bound).

Every Boolean function satisfies

|     |                                |     |
|-----|--------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \deg_{\pm}(f)\leq H^{\ast}(f).
       ```                             |     |

By
Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 (Linear-fractional normal form). ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention"),
an $`H`$-head score is a constant plus a sum of $`H`$ linear-fractional
atoms. Multiplying by the product of their positive affine denominators
preserves its sign pattern on the Boolean cube and yields a polynomial
of degree at most $`H`$.
Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Threshold-Degree Lower Bound ‣ Appendix E Proofs of the Main Results ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives the full argument.

##### Strictness of the lower bound.

The threshold-degree bound is not always tight. For a ten-bit input
$`\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\in\{0,1\}^{10}`$, where
$`\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in\{0,1\}^{5}`$, define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{gathered}Q(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{5}(1-2a_{i})\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{5}(1-2b_{j})\right)-3\sum_{i=1}^{5}\left(1-2a_{i}\right)\left(1-2b_{i}\right),\\
f_{10}(\mathbf{x})=1\Longleftrightarrow Q(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})>0\end{gathered}
``` |  | (6) |

###### Theorem 3 (Strict separation from threshold degree).

The function $`f_{10}`$ satisfies

|     |                                              |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \deg_{\pm}(f_{10})=2<3\leq H^{\ast}(f_{10}).
       ```                                           |     |

Appendix [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Strict Separation from Threshold Degree ‣ Appendix E Proofs of the Main Results ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives the proof. We found autoresearch particularly useful for
constructing examples when the bound in
Theorem [2](#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2 (Threshold-degree lower bound). ‣ Unnormalized attention weights (denominator). ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
is strict, resulting in the example above.

##### Constructive upper bounds.

We next derive a constructive upper bound for functions that depend on a
scalar statistic $`t_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x})`$, in terms of the number of
distinct values that $`t_{\lambda}`$ takes on the Boolean cube.

###### Theorem 4 (Weighted-sum interpolation).

Let $`\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}>0`$ and define
$`t_{\lambda}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}`$ by
$`t_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}x_{i}`$. Suppose
$`f`$ depends on its input only through $`t_{\lambda}`$, so that
$`f(\mathbf{x})=F(t_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}))`$ for some function
$`F:\mathbb{R}\to\{0,1\}`$. Then

|     |                                                    |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       H^{\ast}(f)\leq|\operatorname{Im}(t_{\lambda})|-1.
       ```                                                 |     |

For $`\lambda_{i}=2^{i-1}`$, we have
$`|\operatorname{Im}(t_{\lambda})|=2^{n}`$, so
$`H^{\ast}(f)\leq 2^{n}-1`$ for every Boolean function $`f`$.

The proof uses $`|\operatorname{Im}(t_{\lambda})|-1`$ heads to realize
the labels assigned by $`F`$ to the attainable values of
$`t_{\lambda}`$.
Appendix [E.5](#A5.SS5 "E.5 Weighted-Sum Interpolation ‣ Appendix E Proofs of the Main Results ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives the construction.

### 2.2 Exact Head Complexity for Symmetric Functions

Let $`f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}`$ be symmetric. Equivalently, there is a
unique function $`F:\{0,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,1\}`$ such that, for every
$`\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}`$, $`f(\mathbf{x})=F(|\mathbf{x}|)`$, where
$`|\mathbf{x}|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}`$ ([Paturi, 1992](#bib.bib10)). We
call $`F`$ the *Hamming-weight profile* of $`f`$ and define the number
of changes in this profile by

|     |                                                |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       C(F)=\left|\{k\in[n]:F(k-1)\neq F(k)\}\right|.
       ```                                             |     | (7) |

Taking $`\lambda_{i}=1`$ in
Theorem [4](#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4 (Weighted-sum interpolation). ‣ Constructive upper bounds. ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives $`H^{\ast}(f)\leq n`$. The following result sharpens this bound to
the number of changes in $`F`$.

###### Theorem 5 (Exact symmetric characterization).

For every symmetric Boolean function $`f`$ with Hamming-weight profile
$`F`$,

|     |                                 |     |
|-----|---------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       H^{\ast}(f)=\deg_{\pm}(f)=C(F).
       ```                              |     |

###### Corollary 2 (Parity).

For every $`n\geq 1`$, $`H^{\ast}(\mathrm{PARITY}_{n})=n`$. This follows
from
Theorem [5](#Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 5 (Exact symmetric characterization). ‣ 2.2 Exact Head Complexity for Symmetric Functions ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention"),
since parity has $`n`$ sign changes across Hamming-weight levels.

##### Lower bound.

Lemma 2.6 of [Aspnes et al. (1994)](#bib.bib9) shows that the threshold
degree of a symmetric Boolean function equals the number of changes in
its univariate Hamming-weight representation, so $`\deg_{\pm}(f)=C(F)`$.
Combining this with
Theorem [2](#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2 (Threshold-degree lower bound). ‣ Unnormalized attention weights (denominator). ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives $`H^{\ast}(f)\geq C(F)`$.

##### Upper bound.

We construct a degree-$`C(F)`$ polynomial with sign pattern $`F`$ by
placing one root between each pair of consecutive Hamming-weight levels
at which $`F`$ changes. After dividing this polynomial by a positive
polynomial of the same degree, a partial-fraction decomposition yields a
representation using $`C(F)`$ linear-fractional atoms, so
Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 (Linear-fractional normal form). ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives $`H^{\ast}(f)\leq C(F)`$.
Appendix [E.6](#A5.SS6 "E.6 Exact Symmetric Characterization ‣ Appendix E Proofs of the Main Results ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
gives the full construction.

### 2.3 Machine-Checked Formalization

All results above are formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4. The
codebase lays the groundwork for a publicly available Lean environment
supporting agent-assisted research in mechanistic interpretability.
Section [3](#S3 "3 System Design and Meta-Analysis ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
describes the agents’ contributions and the human review process.

## 3 System Design and Meta-Analysis

The theorems in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
were derived by GPT-5.6 Sol from a /goal prompt. The separation²² 2 A
*separation* is an explicit Boolean function where the threshold degree
is strictly smaller than its head complexity, which shows that the lower
bound of
Theorem [2](#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2 (Threshold-degree lower bound). ‣ Unnormalized attention weights (denominator). ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
is not always tight. in
Theorem [3](#Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3 (Strict separation from threshold degree). ‣ Strictness of the lower bound. ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
was obtained through a separate counterexample search initiated by the
authors. The Lean formalizations were generated through straightforward
prompting, and human researchers subsequently refined the Lean code to
make it legible and reusable. This section is based on the anonymized
record of the autonomous run, released as theorems-rollout.jsonl in the
repository accompanying this paper.³³ 3 The results had already been
obtained in an earlier run. For clarity, this section describes the
rollout of a subsequent run conducted without access to the earlier run,
although its main observations apply to both.

### 3.1 Agent and harness

The theorems in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
were generated by a single GPT-5.6 Sol agent running in a Codex Desktop
sandbox.
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Tools ‣ 3 System Design and Meta-Analysis ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
describes the execution environment. The agent received the problem
setup from
Section [2](#S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1 "Setup ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
and a comprehensive set of acceptance criteria that provided general
research guidance without revealing the expected results. In
approximately 9.5 hours, it derived the linear-fractional normal form
(Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 (Linear-fractional normal form). ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")),
the threshold-degree lower bound
(Theorem [2](#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2 (Threshold-degree lower bound). ‣ Unnormalized attention weights (denominator). ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")),
and the exact symmetric characterization
(Theorem [5](#Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 5 (Exact symmetric characterization). ‣ 2.2 Exact Head Complexity for Symmetric Functions ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")).
The theorem statements, derivations, and supporting constructions were
recorded in answer.md, the run’s primary research output. The agent also
explored broader bounds not reported in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention").
A separate counterexample search subsequently found a 128-bit separation
between threshold degree and head complexity, which was later improved
to the explicit ten-bit example in
Theorem [3](#Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3 (Strict separation from threshold degree). ‣ Strictness of the lower bound. ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention").

##### Defining the problem.

Considerable human effort went into specifying the research question
precisely and fixing a model against which proposed results could be
audited.
Appendices [F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 Problem statement at the start of the run ‣ Appendix F Initial Prompt and Repository README of the Autonomous Run ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
and [F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Model specification at the start of the run ‣ Appendix F Initial Prompt and Repository README of the Autonomous Run ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
reproduce the problem statement and model specification, respectively.
Since a closed-form characterization of $`H^{\ast}(f)`$ for arbitrary
Boolean functions could not be assumed, the problem statement identified
several broader forms of progress, including lower and upper bounds,
comparisons with classical complexity measures, and exact results for
natural function families.

##### The theorem-generation prompt.

The prompt, adapted from [OpenAI (2026)](#bib.bib30), asked the agent to
conduct a diversified search across multiple proof strategies. It was
submitted through Codex’s /goal command, which maintains a persistent
objective and completion condition across turns ([Pathak and Fabbri,
2026](#bib.bib31)). The prompt instructed the agent to explore genuinely
different proof strategies, organize them by their underlying
mathematical ideas, and support them with concrete equations or
counterexamples. Public web search was disabled so that the agent could
not retrieve existing solutions during the run. The run was one-shot:
after receiving the initial prompt, the agent completed the search and
returned its answer without further human input.
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Initial Prompt and Repository README of the Autonomous Run ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
reproduces the prompt verbatim.

The run used a single gpt-5.6-sol process at xhigh reasoning effort in
Codex Desktop. Session metadata records Codex CLI build
0.148.0-alpha.21, source vscode, a 258,400-token context window, and
four context compactions. Although the multi-agent runtime was
available, the agent did not spawn any subagents. It used no external
connectors and did not invoke Lean during the initial research interval.
Lean was introduced only after a subsequent user request because the
initial run focused on developing the theory in natural language.

##### The /goal command alone was insufficient.

In preliminary runs, supplying only a /goal objective led the agent to
stop after a short period, make only incremental progress, and mark the
goal as complete prematurely. Adapting the persistence and search
instructions from [OpenAI (2026)](#bib.bib30) was therefore important
for sustaining a longer research run.

##### Counterexample-search setup.

The counterexample search used a separate Codex Desktop session with a
single GPT-5.6 Sol agent running at ultra reasoning effort. Its first
turn comprised 32 tool calls completed in under seven minutes.
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Human interventions ‣ 3 System Design and Meta-Analysis ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
describes how the search was initiated and refined.

### 3.2 Tools

The run used Python 3, NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, and standard shell and Git
tools for numerical experiments, symbolic and exact calculations,
repository inspection, and testing.
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Tools ‣ 3 System Design and Meta-Analysis ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
summarizes the recorded shell activity. Based on command syntax, we
classified 373 of the 387 calls and left the remaining 14 unclassified
rather than infer their purpose from context. The empirical checks
tested the main constructions in answer.md using exact arithmetic and
exhaustive evaluation on small instances; the other classified calls
included additional checks on small Boolean functions and the proposed
upper-bound constructions.

| Command category          | Calls |
|---------------------------|-------|
| Python invocations        | 153   |
| sed inspections           | 70    |
| rg searches               | 40    |
| Runs of empirical checks  | 24    |
| Numbered file inspections | 17    |
| Git queries               | 14    |
| Other classified calls    | 55    |
| Unclassified calls        | 14    |
| Total                     | 387   |

Table 1: Recorded shell activity during the theorem-generation run.

##### Sandboxing details.

The run executed in a Codex Desktop sandbox on a local Linux virtual
machine: a managed permission profile with read access to the whole file
system, write access only to the project directory and temporary
directories, and no network access. Any action outside these bounds
would have required the user’s approval, and the rollout records no such
request before delivery. Its computations were exact or small-scale
numerical checks.

##### Details on the counterexample search.

The counterexample search that reduced the initial 128-bit construction
to the ten-bit example in
Theorem [3](#Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3 (Strict separation from threshold degree). ‣ Strictness of the lower bound. ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
used Python and exact solvers for small Boolean instances, with public
web search available. The formalization was carried out in Lean 4 using
Mathlib and Lake, with computationally intensive builds run on an
institutional SLURM cluster.

### 3.3 Research loop

The run proceeded in two stages. The agent spent approximately 9 hours
and 38 minutes developing the proofs and producing answer.md. It then
completed the Lean formalization and committed the results in a further
22 minutes. These timings come from the retained platform event log and
include tool latency and idle time.

|  Measure |  Summary |
|----|----|
|  Messages |  intermediate assistant messages and one final answer. The context was compacted four times. |
|  Tool use |  The log records 949 tool calls and 960 operations within those calls. The latter comprise 387 shell commands, 307 file edits, 205 continuations of shell sessions, 55 goal checks, and six goal or plan updates. |
|  Token use |  The platform reported about 142.4 million cumulative input tokens, of which 140.2 million were cached, and 0.64 million output tokens, including 0.32 million reasoning tokens. |
|  Research process |  The agent registered thirteen approach families and used no public web search, external connector, or delegated model call. |

Table 2: Summary of the autonomous theorem-generation run. Token counts
are taken from the last record before the final answer and therefore
exclude that turn.

Input-token usage is cumulative across model calls, so retained context
is counted repeatedly. Of the 142.4 million input tokens recorded, 98.5%
were retrieved from the prompt cache.

##### Exploring proof strategies.

During the run, the agent tracked different approaches in
approach_registry.md.
Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Exploring proof strategies. ‣ 3.3 Research loop ‣ 3 System Design and Meta-Analysis ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention")
groups these approaches by their goals and summarizes their outcomes.

|  Goal |  Approach |  Outcome |
|----|----|----|
|  Reformulate head complexity |  Replace the full matrix parameterization with a scalar description of each head’s contribution. |  Derived Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 (Linear-fractional normal form). ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention"). |
|  Prove upper bounds |  Construct representations for functions determined by weighted sums and for symmetric functions. |  Derived Theorems [4](#Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4 (Weighted-sum interpolation). ‣ Constructive upper bounds. ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention") and [5](#Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 5 (Exact symmetric characterization). ‣ 2.2 Exact Head Complexity for Symmetric Functions ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention"), plus bounds not included in the paper. |
|  Prove lower bounds |  Compare head complexity with threshold degree and study functions that require more heads. |  Derived Theorem [2](#Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 2 (Threshold-degree lower bound). ‣ Unnormalized attention weights (denominator). ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention") and additional lower-bound arguments. |
|  Evaluate candidate approaches |  Check proposed identities and constructions on finite instances. |  Rejected approaches that failed finite checks and set aside those that still required an unproved lemma. |

Table 3: High-level summary of the proof families explored during the
run.

The agent kept several distinct approaches under consideration rather
than committing early to a single line of attack. Patterns observed in
small cases were not treated as general results unless the remaining
proof steps could be completed. When further exact checks produced
counterexamples or showed that a proposed construction could not cover
all cases, the corresponding approach was marked as blocked. This
process prevented several plausible but unsupported generalizations from
entering the final answer.

### 3.4 Human interventions

##### Theorem generation.

The initial prompt specified the problem and the criteria for a complete
answer. From the submission of this prompt to the delivery of answer.md,
the agent received no further human input, mathematical lemmas, or
corrections.

##### Lean formalization.

After the theorem-generation run, the authors asked the agent to commit
the artifacts and formalize the core results in Lean. The generated code
captured the intended results but was not initially organized for
readability or reuse. Human researchers selected the final theorem set,
checked that the Lean statements matched the intended claims, and
restructured the code to improve its naming, documentation, and use of
the existing library.

##### Counterexample search.

The decision to search for an explicit counterexample came from the
authors. No such example had emerged during the autonomous
theorem-generation runs. Given the one-line goal *find an explicit
constructive example when $`\deg_{\pm}(f)`$ is not equal to
$`H^{\ast}(f)`$*, the agent’s first turn proceeded without further human
input and produced a 128-bit example. In subsequent turns, the authors
asked the agent to explain candidate examples, find progressively
smaller examples with a Lean-friendly proof, and formalize the result in
the shared repository. The search ultimately yielded the ten-bit
function in
Theorem [3](#Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 3 (Strict separation from threshold degree). ‣ Strictness of the lower bound. ‣ 2.1.1 Why the correspondence holds ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention").

### 3.5 Verification

We rely on the Lean formalization to verify the reported theorems. The
Lean kernel checks each proof, while a Lean expert checks that its
formal statement faithfully captures the meaning, assumptions, and scope
of the corresponding natural-language claim. This guards against
hallucinated proofs. Future work could incorporate Lean’s comparator
tool to check untrusted, agent-generated proofs against human-reviewed
theorem statements in a sandboxed environment ([Lean FRO,
2026](#bib.bib34)).

### 3.6 Significance of result

The mathematical result treats the number of attention heads as an
architectural resource and exactly characterizes the head count required
to represent symmetric Boolean functions. It provides a tractable
setting for studying architectural expressivity without modeling
training dynamics. More generally, it establishes threshold degree as a
lower bound on head complexity while showing that this lower bound need
not be tight. These results therefore provide a mathematical reference
point for asking whether a computation observed across several heads in
a trained toy model is required by the architecture or reflects a
particular solution found through training.

The broader program is to develop component-level results of this kind
into mathematical abstractions for tracking features through attention,
feed-forward networks, and multiple layers. Such abstractions could
provide principled starting points for empirical studies and,
eventually, inform feature-discovery tools for larger transformers. Many
current feature-decomposition methods, including sparse autoencoders,
learn features from model activations without constraining those
features by the computations that the transformer’s architecture can
implement ([Cunningham et al., 2023](#bib.bib17); [Shafran et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)).

An architecture-aware probe could instead ask how many attention heads
are required to construct a given feature in a single attention-layer
update. The linear-fractional normal form in
Theorem [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1 (Linear-fractional normal form). ‣ 2.1 Characterizing Head Complexity ‣ 2 Autonomous Research Result ‣ Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention"),
which characterizes the contribution realizable by one attention head,
provides a theoretical starting point for developing such a probe. The
present result is an initial step: it gives exact statements for a
one-layer attention only transformer rather than demonstrating transfer
to trained models at scale.

Together, the mathematical results and their Lean formalization give
other mechanistic interpretability researchers a concrete artifact to
reuse and extend. Although the current development is limited to the
one-layer Boolean setting studied here, it lays the groundwork for a
reusable formal environment in which related questions about transformer
components can be stated and verified.

### 3.7 Interpretability

During the autonomous theorem-generation run, the agent maintained a
registry of approaches and their status, and executable scripts for
computational checks. The platform recorded prompts, assistant messages
and tool calls that can be useful when we want to audit the autoresearch
run. Together, these records allow the research trajectory to be
reconstructed, including why some approaches were completed or
abandoned.

### 3.8 Limitations

##### Auditability of autonomous research.

The volume of reasoning and results produced during long autonomous runs
makes their progress difficult to inspect and steer. Determining which
approaches advanced, failed, or were abandoned requires substantial
review. Tools that summarize research branches and track the status of
claims could reduce this burden and help researchers identify where
human guidance would be most useful.

##### Repetition and premature claims of progress.

Extended runs can produce repetitive updates and apparent progress that
does not survive scrutiny. The retained rollout contains prolonged
monitoring of stalled searches, an incorrect explanation repeated before
correction, and a proposed new bound later removed because an existing
bound was stronger. These episodes added work without a corresponding
improvement in the final result. A monitor that tracks new evidence,
flags repetitive or unsupported claims, and recommends redirection or
stopping could help guide the search. Whether such monitoring improves
research outcomes remains untested.

Together, these limitations motivate treating autoresearch itself as an
object of scientific study. Controlled comparisons of prompts, tools,
monitoring, human steering, and stopping rules are needed to determine
which workflows produce reliable results and how much computational and
human effort they require.

## 4 Broader Impact

##### Societal benefits and risks.

This work contributes to a longer-term effort to make transformer
behavior more understandable and amenable to oversight. Precise results
about architectural expressivity can provide foundations for
interpretability methods, which may eventually help researchers identify
and investigate undesirable model behavior by designing theoretically
grounded feature-decomposition tools. These benefits remain prospective:
our theorems concern exact representation in a one-layer attention only
model and do not establish safety guarantees for deployed systems.
Furthermore, the research process in this work serves as a proof of
concept for mechanistic interpretability researchers who want to pursue
mathematically demanding questions but lack ready access to
collaborators with expertise in mathematical research or formal theorem
proving.

##### Scientific judgment.

Autonomous theorem discovery leaves a central role for human scientific
judgment, both in asking informative questions and in assessing the
resulting claims. Since the overarching question is broad and has no
obvious route to a complete answer, researchers must choose tractable
idealizations that isolate meaningful aspects of transformer computation
that can inform empirical interpretability. While the state of the art
agents are good at solving well defined problems, it remains for the
researcher to ask the high level questions and guide the autoresearch
runs.

##### Understanding failures and steering autoresearch.

We need to understand its failure modes and how to steer it, especially
for open-ended theoretical questions, where no obvious scalar metric
captures scientific progress. We propose adapting Inspect ([UK AI
Security Institute, 2024](#bib.bib32)) and Inspect Scout ([Dubois et
al., 2026](#bib.bib33)) to audit research runs through their logs. A
monitoring agent built on this infrastructure could track verified
intermediate results and flag repeated attempts that do not contribute
to research progress.

## Appendix A Reproducibility Statement

All results in this work are accompanied by a public repository
available at
[https://github.com/VerifiedMechanisms/automlr](https://github.com/VerifiedMechanisms/automlr).
The natural-language theorem statements and proofs are collected in the
top-level theorems/ directory. The corresponding machine-checked Lean 4
development is contained in formalization/. The theorem-generation and
counterexample-search records are released in system-design/rollouts/.
Build and proof-integrity checks are documented in
formalization/README.md and formalization/BUILDING.md.

The repository is self contained and no external datasets are required
to reproduce the results. The authors did the 9.5 hour autoresearch run
using a ChatGPT Pro plan. The machine-checked results in this work are
done using Lean 4.31.0 and Mathlib 4.31.0. Refer to the README.md in the
accompanying repository for detailed instructions.
````
